pages.title: Why can the same bond respond differently?

blocks.text: A multiple bond has electrons that can respond to an approaching reagent, while an alkyl group can help stabilise a neighbouring electron-deficient centre. We need to distinguish these effects before turning to a separate practical question: how to isolate a pure organic product.

This unit follows the mapped NCERT sequence: the electromeric effect, hyperconjugation and then basic purification methods. Electron effects explain reactivity; purification exploits measurable physical differences such as solubility and boiling point. Neither requires memorising an unexplained list of names.

pages.transition: First examine the temporary π-electron response to a reagent.

pages.title: Electromeric effect: a temporary response

blocks.text: The electromeric effect is the complete displacement of a multiple bond’s π-electron pair towards one atom under the influence of an attacking reagent. It is temporary and disappears when the influence is removed without reaction. It concerns π electrons, unlike the inductive effect in σ bonds.

When H⁺ approaches an alkene, a π pair can be used to make a C–H bond. The electrons move towards the atom that bonds to the attacking reagent: the +E description. When a nucleophile attacks a carbonyl carbon, the π pair shifts towards oxygen, away from the attacked carbon: −E.

Volatile means able to form vapour readily. Solubility describes how much of a substance dissolves in a given solvent under stated conditions. These properties depend on temperature and on the substances involved.

pages.transition: A neighbouring σ bond can stabilise a reactive centre in a different way.

pages.title: A neighbouring sigma bond can stabilise a cation

blocks.text: Hyperconjugation is delocalisation involving a σ bond, commonly C–H, next to an empty p orbital or a π system. The orbitals must be suitably aligned. Sharing electron density over a larger region helps stabilise the species rather than keeping all electron deficiency concentrated at one carbon.

In CH3CH2+, the empty p orbital on CH2+ can interact with C–H σ bonds on the adjacent CH3 group. The carbon–hydrogen bonds are not actually breaking to release free H⁺; the “no-bond” contributors are a way of describing delocalisation.

pages.transition: Counting adjacent C–H bonds makes this stabilisation argument concrete.

pages.title: Count adjacent bonds, not just carbon atoms

blocks.text: Compare CH3CH2+, (CH3)2CH⁺ and (CH3)3C+. Their directly neighbouring methyl groups provide 3, 6 and 9 adjacent C–H bonds respectively for hyperconjugative interaction. Together with inductive donation this supports the simple alkyl-cation order tertiary > secondary > primary.

The isopropyl cation is (CH3)2CH⁺, not CH3CH2+. The latter is ethyl. Methyl cation, CH3⁺, has no adjacent carbon and therefore no adjacent C–H bonds for this interaction. Apply this comparison to simple alkyl cations; resonance may alter comparisons in other families.

pages.transition: After a reaction, a new problem remains: separating the product from impurities.

pages.title: Purity is needed before identification

blocks.text: An isolated reaction mixture can contain the desired compound, reactants, solvent and by-products. A measured melting or boiling point is useful for identification only after suitable purification. Choose a separation method from a physical difference between the product and its impurities.

A volatile liquid mixed with a non-volatile solid suggests distillation. A solid much more soluble in hot solvent than cold solvent suggests crystallisation. A sublimable solid with a non-sublimable impurity suggests sublimation. The same method is not appropriate for every mixture.

pages.transition: For solids, sublimation and changing solubility offer two useful contrasts.

pages.title: Sublimation and crystallisation

blocks.text: Sublimation changes a solid directly into vapour without passing through a liquid phase; cooling recovers the solid. Crystallisation dissolves an impure solid in a suitable hot solvent and forms purer crystals on cooling, using differences in solubility.

For crystallisation, use a solvent that dissolves the product well when hot but poorly when cold. Insoluble impurities are removed from the hot solution; soluble impurities can remain in the mother liquor, the liquid left after crystallisation. Washing crystals with a small amount of cold solvent limits product loss.

pages.transition: For liquids, volatility provides a different separation principle.

pages.title: Why simple distillation works

blocks.text: Distillation vaporises a liquid and condenses its vapour. It separates a volatile liquid from non-volatile impurities or liquids with a sufficiently large boiling-point difference. The more volatile component enriches the vapour that is collected first.

NCERT compares chloroform, boiling near 334 K, with aniline, boiling near 457 K. Their widely separated boiling points support simple distillation. Boiling a mixture is not itself purification: the vapour must be condensed and collected separately under appropriate laboratory conditions.

pages.transition: When boiling points are close, a single vaporisation is often insufficient.

pages.title: Close boiling points need repeated separation

blocks.text: Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column between the boiling flask and condenser. Repeated condensation and vaporisation within the column enrich the more volatile component more effectively than a single vaporisation. It is useful when liquid boiling points are close.

Petroleum separation uses this principle on an industrial scale. The fractions represent ranges of boiling points rather than necessarily pure single compounds. The column improves separation; it does not make all components have different boiling points or chemically convert them into new substances.

pages.transition: If heating itself damages the product, pressure becomes another useful control.

pages.title: Lowering pressure protects a sensitive liquid

blocks.text: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. Lower external pressure therefore allows boiling at a lower temperature. Distillation under reduced pressure is useful for high-boiling liquids or substances that would decompose near their normal boiling points.

Glycerol can be purified under reduced pressure rather than heating it to its high normal boiling temperature. This is a pressure–boiling-point choice, not a claim that the molecule becomes more thermally stable. Purification procedures require supervised laboratory equipment, especially heating and pressure control.

A product may need more than one purification step. Distillation can remove a solvent, followed by crystallisation of a solid product if a suitable hot–cold solubility contrast exists. A method should be chosen for the mixture at that stage, rather than assigned permanently to a compound name.

pages.transition: We can now match each electron effect and separation method to its proper purpose.

pages.title: Match the explanation to the question

blocks.text: The electromeric effect concerns a reagent-induced π-pair displacement; hyperconjugation concerns stabilising delocalisation from a neighbouring σ bond. Preserve the actual intermediate’s formula and count adjacent C–H bonds when using the simple stability argument.

For separation, identify the useful physical difference: sublimation, hot–cold solubility, volatility, close boiling points or thermal sensitivity. Crystallisation needs an appropriate solvent; fractional distillation adds repeated separation; reduced pressure lowers the temperature required for boiling.

questions.question: How does the electromeric effect differ from induction?
questions.answer: It is temporary and involves complete π-pair displacement under a reagent’s influence; induction is permanent polarisation through σ bonds.

questions.question: How many adjacent methyl C–H bonds are available in (CH3)2CH⁺?
questions.answer: Six: two adjacent CH3 groups each supply three. The positively charged carbon itself is not the methyl group being counted.

questions.question: Why can cold washing be preferable when collecting crystals?
questions.answer: The product is less soluble in cold solvent, so washing removes adhering impurities while limiting loss of product.

questions.question: What extra function does a fractionating column provide?
questions.answer: Repeated vaporisation and condensation enrich the more volatile component, helping separate close-boiling liquids.

questions.question: Why use reduced pressure for a decomposing high-boiling liquid?
questions.answer: Boiling occurs at a lower temperature when external pressure is lowered, avoiding excessive heating near its normal boiling point.
